proof:
1. Notation. λ is Lebesgue measure on ℝ and λ_I := λ⌞(σ, ρ], a finite measure (λ((σ, ρ]) = max(ρ − σ, 0) < ∞); ν_S := ν⌞S, which is s-finite because ν is. For t ∈ ℝ put T_t := {x ∈ X : t < r(x)}, and put T := {(t, x) ∈ ℝ × X : t < r(x)}. All integrals are Bochner (Lebesgue) integrals of real-valued functions; Fubini's theorem is applied below only to an integrable function on the product.
2. Measurability. The maps (t, x) ↦ t and (t, x) ↦ r(x) are measurable on ℝ × X with the product σ-algebra, so T = {(t, x) : t < r(x)} is measurable. Likewise every T_t = r⁻¹((t, ∞)) is measurable in X, and every interval (−∞, u) is Borel in ℝ.
3. Product integrand. Let Ψ(t, x) := F′(t)g(x) and Φ := 1_T·Ψ, i.e. Φ(t, x) = F′(t)g(x) if t < r(x) and Φ(t, x) = 0 otherwise. Since F′ ∈ L¹(λ_I) and g ∈ L¹(ν_S), Ψ is λ_I ⊗ ν_S-integrable: it is a.e.-strongly measurable as the product of an a.e.-strongly measurable function of t and one of x, and by Tonelli's theorem (valid for s-finite factors) ∫∫|Ψ| d(λ_I ⊗ ν_S) = (∫_{(σ,ρ]}|F′|dλ)·(∫_S|g|dν) < ∞. Because T is measurable (step 2), Φ = 1_T·Ψ is also λ_I ⊗ ν_S-integrable.
4. Fubini. Both factors λ_I and ν_S are s-finite and Φ ∈ L¹(λ_I ⊗ ν_S), so Fubini's theorem, which holds for s-finite (not only σ-finite) factors, gives: (i) x ↦ ∫Φ(t, x)dλ_I(t) is ν_S-integrable; (ii) t ↦ ∫Φ(t, x)dν_S(x) is λ_I-integrable; (iii) ∫(∫Φ(t, x)dν_S(x))dλ_I(t) = ∫(∫Φ(t, x)dλ_I(t))dν_S(x).
5. Sections at fixed t. For all t ∈ ℝ and x ∈ X, Φ(t, x) = F′(t)·(1_{T_t}g)(x). Pulling out the constant F′(t) and using that T_t is measurable (step 2), ∫Φ(t, x)dν_S(x) = F′(t)∫_S 1_{T_t}g dν = F′(t)∫_{S∩T_t} g dν for every t ∈ ℝ.
6. Sections at fixed x ∈ S. For x ∈ S and t ∈ ℝ, Φ(t, x) = g(x)·(1_{(−∞, r(x))}F′)(t). Hence ∫Φ(t, x)dλ_I(t) = g(x)∫_{(σ,ρ]∩(−∞,r(x))} F′dλ. Because r(x) ∈ (σ, ρ] we have (σ, ρ] ∩ (−∞, r(x)) = (σ, r(x)) (if σ < t < r(x) then t < ρ). The sets (σ, r(x)) and (σ, r(x)] differ by the λ-null set {r(x)}, so ∫_{(σ,r(x))}F′ = ∫_{(σ,r(x)]}F′, and the hypothesis on F at the point t = r(x) ∈ (σ, ρ] ⊆ [σ, ρ] gives ∫_{(σ,r(x)]}F′ = F(r(x)) − F(σ). Therefore ∫Φ(t, x)dλ_I(t) = g(x)(F(r(x)) − F(σ)) for every x ∈ S.
7. Conclusion (a). By step 6 the ν_S-integrable function of step 4(i) coincides with x ↦ g(x)(F(r(x)) − F(σ)) at every point of S. Since S is measurable, ν_S-almost every point lies in S, so the two functions are ν_S-a.e. equal; hence x ↦ g(x)(F(r(x)) − F(σ)) is ν-integrable on S.
8. Conclusion (b). By step 5 the λ_I-integrable function of step 4(ii) equals t ↦ F′(t)∫_{S∩T_t} g dν at every t ∈ ℝ, so the latter is Lebesgue integrable on (σ, ρ].
9. Conclusion (c). ∫_{(σ,ρ]}F′(t)(∫_{S∩T_t} g dν)dt = ∫(∫Φ(t, x)dν_S(x))dλ_I(t) by step 5, = ∫(∫Φ(t, x)dλ_I(t))dν_S(x) by step 4(iii), = ∫_S g(x)(F(r(x)) − F(σ))dν(x) by step 6, because the two integrands agree at every point of the measurable set S. ∎
key_steps: T := {(t, x) : t < r(x)} is product-measurable and Φ(t, x) := 1_T(t, x)F′(t)g(x) is integrable for λ⌞(σ,ρ] ⊗ ν⌞S, being the restriction to T of the integrable product F′(t)g(x)
Fubini: both partial integrals of Φ are integrable and the two iterated integrals agree
t-section: ∫Φ(t, ·)dν⌞S = F′(t)∫_{S∩{t<r}} g dν for every t
x-section for x ∈ S: (σ, ρ] ∩ (−∞, r(x)) = (σ, r(x)); drop the null endpoint r(x) and use F(r(x)) = F(σ) + ∫_{(σ,r(x)]}F′ to get g(x)(F(r(x)) − F(σ))
Transfer the integrability statements and the identity through the two section formulas (a.e. on ν⌞S, pointwise in t)
